query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Optimizing the laser’s linear energy density during selective laser melting (SLM) of refractory high‐entropy alloys will improve dimensional precision and in situ mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication‐induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy (e.g., NbMoTaW) fabricated by SLM using conventional (sub‐optimal) laser parameters that yield nonuniform melting, leading to dimensional deviations and a higher concentration of porosity and microstructural defects.
generation.intervention: Adjust the SLM process to target a linear energy density near 2.83 J/mm by tuning laser power and scan speed.
generation.conditions: The intervention is applied during laser powder bed fusion in an inert atmosphere on refractory HEA powders with high melting points under otherwise standard processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A more uniform, single-phase BCC solid solution with reduced thermal gradients and a stabilized melt pool during solidification.
generation.mechanism: By fine-tuning the energy input, thermal gradients and residual stresses are minimized, thereby stabilizing the melt pool and promoting complete melting and rapid, uniform solidification. This reduces porosity and other fabrication-induced defects, resulting in better dimensional control and improved mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline process, parts produced with the optimized linear energy density will exhibit dimensions that more closely match their design specifications, a lower density of defects (e.g., porosity, microcracks), and enhanced mechanical properties such as increased microhardness.
generation.baseline: Additively manufactured refractory HEA components produced using conventional, less-optimized SLM parameters that result in significant thermal gradients and associated fabrication defects.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold for refractory HEAs processed via SLM where the melt pool dynamics are primarily governed by controllable energy input; however, different alloy systems or additive manufacturing methods may not show similar improvements.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of improvements in dimensional precision and mechanical properties may vary with additional factors including powder quality, machine calibration, and environmental conditions during SLM.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of refractory HEA samples via SLM: one using the conventional (baseline) energy settings and the other using the optimized parameters targeting a linear energy density of ~2.83 J/mm. Ensure all other processing conditions (powder type, ambient atmosphere, etc.) are held constant.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy measurements (comparing final part dimensions to CAD specifications)
Defect density evaluation through microscopy or CT scanning (to quantify porosity and crack presence)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the optimized-energy samples do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional accuracy, reduced defect density, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have excellent mechanical properties, which could make them the substitutes of some superalloys. However, the high melting point of refractory HEAs leads to processing problems when using traditional processing techniques. In this study, a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW alloy was formed by selective laser melting (SLM) with a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. The composition distribution was analyzed, and the element with a lower melting point and lower density showed a negative deviation (no more than 5%) of the molar ratio in the formed alloy. The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys, making it a new substitute metal with great application prospects in aerospace and energy fields.
